payload.claim: In a backtest of four SPY allocation approaches over January 2000–August 2025, the approach that produced the lowest drawdown also produced a lower growth-of-$1 outcome than a fully-invested (buy-and-hold) SPY approach.
payload.quote:
The growth of $1 across four SPY allocation approaches, January 2000–August 2025. All four lines come from the historical backtest discussed in the article.
I wanted to know how much difference a simple, mechanical change in equity exposure would have made over a full cycle. I tested four portfolio rules on more than 25 years of daily SPY data. The lowest-drawdown approach cushioned the worst losses, but an investor who followed it ended up with less money than someone who stayed fully invested. The trade-off is substantial enough to deserve a close look.

data_required: SPY daily price data, January 2000 to August 2025
testability.notes: Exact rules defining the four approaches are not specified in this excerpt, limiting full reproducibility, but the sample window, instrument, and core result (lowest-drawdown underperforms buy-and-hold) are stated.

payload.claim: Using recent price volatility and a longer-term market trend measure individually, and then combined, to adjust SPY equity exposure produces different outcomes in the backtest, with volatility reacting quickly to shocks and the trend measure capturing slower deterioration.
payload.quote: The exercise begins with two familiar pieces of information: recent price volatility and the longer-term market trend. Volatility can rise quickly during a shock; a trend measure can pick up a slower deterioration. I tested what each contributes, then what happens when the two are used together.

source.title: Can You Reduce Risk Without Missing the Rally?

testability.notes: No specific parameter values (lookback windows, thresholds) are given in this passage, reducing precision; the claim is stated at the generality the quote supports.

payload.claim: Executing the same order (holding participation rate and order size constant) in the final hour of the trading session is consistently less costly than executing it earlier in the day.
payload.quote: The findings indicate that executing the same order in the final hour of the trading session is consistently less costly than executing it earlier in the day.

source.title: Optimizing trading cost by leveraging "The Time of Day Effect"July 29, 2025In this article, we examine how trading costs vary throughout the day, independent of volume, revealing a persistent Time of Day Effect.

payload.claim: For Russell 2000 constituent stocks, simulating trades of 1% of daily volume at a fixed 15% participation rate using TAQ data shows that trading costs decline substantially as the session progresses, with the lowest market impact observed in the final two hours of the trading day.
payload.quote: To quantify this effect we used Trade and Quote (TAQ) data to simulate trading 1% of daily volume in Russell 2000 constituent stocks at a fixed 15% participation rate. Figure 1 illustrates this effect, highlighting distinct cost profiles throughout the day. The analysis reveals that trading costs decline substantially as the session progresses, with the lowest market impact observed in the final two hours.

source.title: Optimizing trading cost by leveraging "The Time of Day Effect"July 29, 2025In this article, we examine how trading costs vary throughout the day, independent of volume, revealing a persistent Time of Day Effect.

payload.claim: Time of day exerts an independent and significant influence on execution cost beyond participation rate, and intraday volume does not fully explain where and when liquidity is cheapest.
payload.quote: These results suggest that participation rate alone does not determine execution cost. Time of day exerts an independent and significant influence. While most execution algorithms use intraday volume as a proxy for liquidity, the data shows that volume does not fully explain where and when liquidity is cheapest.

source.title: Optimizing trading cost by leveraging "The Time of Day Effect"July 29, 2025In this article, we examine how trading costs vary throughout the day, independent of volume, revealing a persistent Time of Day Effect.

testability.notes: Qualitative interpretive claim derived from the TAQ simulation results described elsewhere in the document.

payload.claim: An analysis of approximately 635,000 live parent orders over four years of trading (excluding canceled and passive limit orders) comparing full-day orders to those initiated in the final hour of the session corroborates the finding that final-hour execution has lower cost.
payload.quote: To validate these results with live execution data, we analyzed approximately 635,000 parent orders from four years of trading, excluding canceled and passive limit orders. We compared full-day orders with those initiated in the final hour of the session and it corroborates the TAQ-based findings, in striking fashion.

source.title: Optimizing trading cost by leveraging "The Time of Day Effect"July 29, 2025In this article, we examine how trading costs vary throughout the day, independent of volume, revealing a persistent Time of Day Effect.

payload.claim: A finite mixture normal regression applied to more than 172,000 firm-year observations spanning 1963 to 2022 reveals latent group structure in the asset growth-return relation.
payload.quote: Using data on more than 172,000 firm-year observations from 1963 to 2022, they let the model find its own structure.

source.title: What Really Drives the Asset Growth Anomaly? New Evidence Points to Mispricing, Not Risk

data_required: firm-year asset growth and return panel 1963-2022
testability.notes: Testable via replication of FMNR methodology, though technique is complex.

payload.claim: A two-latent-group finite mixture normal regression model of the asset growth-return relation fits firm-year return data decisively better than a single-group model, with BIC declining by more than 10,000 when moving from one to two groups.
payload.quote: The result: the data clearly prefer two latent groups over one. Model fit — measured by log-likelihood, Akaike Information Criterion (a simple score that helps you pick the best model from a set of candidates by balancing how well the model fits the data against how complicated the model is), and Bayesian Information Criterion (similar in spirit to AIC but with a stronger penalty for complexity, especially when you have a lot of data) — improves dramatically when moving from a single group to two groups, with the BIC declining by more than 10,000, far past the threshold that constitutes decisive statistical evidence for the more complex model.

source.title: What Really Drives the Asset Growth Anomaly? New Evidence Points to Mispricing, Not Risk

data_required: firm-year asset growth and return panel 1963-2022

payload.claim: In one latent subgroup of firms, next-year returns are highest in the most extreme asset-shrinkage and asset-growth quintiles and lowest in the middle (U-shaped), while in a second latent subgroup returns are lowest at the extremes and least negative in the middle (inverted U-shaped).
payload.quote: In the first latent group, the relation between asset growth and next-year returns is clearly U-shaped: returns are highest for the most extreme asset-shrinkage and asset-growth quintiles, and lowest in the middle. In the second latent group, the pattern flips into an inverted U: returns are lowest at the extremes and least negative in the middle.

source.locator: What the Two Groups Look Like section
source.title: What Really Drives the Asset Growth Anomaly? New Evidence Points to Mispricing, Not Risk

payload.claim: In both the U-shaped and inverted-U-shaped latent return groups, the downward-sloping segment of the asset growth-return relation is steeper than the upward-sloping segment, and this asymmetry generates the net negative asset growth-return relation observed in the overall sample.
payload.quote: Critically, in both groups, the pattern is asymmetric. The downward-sloping segment is steeper than the upward-sloping segment in both the U-shaped and inverted U-shaped groups. That asymmetry is what generates a net negative asset growth-return relation overall — the familiar anomaly — even though the underlying relation within each group is nonlinear rather than a simple downward slope.

payload.quote:
Run the whole sample through a standard single-group
regression
(the way most of the existing literature does it) and you get exactly the well-known monotonic decline in returns across asset growth quintiles. The nonlinearity and the two-regime structure are invisible unless you go looking for them.

payload.quote:
Risk adjustment.
They strip out each firm’s exposure to 10 established risk factors — including CMA itself, along with momentum and four factors explicitly built to capture mispricing and behavioral effects. If the pattern were really compensation for risk, this adjustment should make it disappear. It doesn’t: the U-shaped and inverted U-shaped patterns, and their asymmetry, survive largely intact.

Price-to-value validation.
Using the same price-to-value estimates from their earlier analysis, they show that firms with higher price-to-value ratios (more likely overvalued) are significantly more likely to be assigned by the model to the inverted-U group — exactly what the mispricing story predicts, and a useful external check on whether the statistically-identified groups actually correspond to over- and under-valued firms.

payload.text:
crypto-grid-record-v1: The record of which crypto cells are searched, fixed before any result from them exists. A cell is one asset at one timeframe. This note fixes the whole grid of crypto cells now, in three phases, so that nothing is added to it after results begin to arrive. It changes no existing verdict, moves no strategy, and re-judges nothing on the chain. Until this entry the crypto class was searched as one pooled two-asset book, BTCUSD and ETHUSD together at 1d, one spec per sweep combination. From this entry crypto is searched cell by cell, one single-asset spec per sweep combination, per active cell, as every other asset class already is.

THE ADMISSION LINE. A crypto asset is admitted only if its first daily bar falls on or before 2022-12-31, which is at least 365 days of history before the 2023-12-31 screen cutoff. The line was set by Coen on 2026-10-17, before any result from these cells exists, and applies to every asset alike. 76 declared assets meet it. 24 do not, and none of the 24 is a cell in any phase.

THE GRID.

Phase 1 cells (active from this entry): timeframe 1d on assets: BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, BNBUSDT, XRPUSDT, SOLUSDT, TRXUSDT, ZECUSDT, DOGEUSDT, LINKUSDT, ADAUSDT, XLMUSDT, BCHUSDT, LTCUSDT, HBARUSDT, AVAXUSDT, SHIBUSDT, UNIUSDT, NEARUSDT, PAXGUSDT, AAVEUSDT, DOTUSDT, ICPUSDT, ETCUSDT, QNTUSDT, NEXOUSDT, ALGOUSDT, ATOMUSDT, JSTUSDT, VETUSDT, FILUSDT, CAKEUSDT, INJUSDT, STXUSDT, DASHUSDT, CRVUSDT, APTUSDT, FETUSDT, SUNUSDT, GNOUSDT, LDOUSDT, LUNCUSDT, XTZUSDT, ENSUSDT, CFXUSDT, DCRUSDT, JASMYUSDT, RAYUSDT, CVXUSDT, OPUSDT, IOTAUSDT, COMPUSDT, TWTUSDT, GRTUSDT, THETAUSDT, RUNEUSDT, AXSUSDT, NEOUSDT, CHZUSDT, MANAUSDT, APEUSDT, XECUSDT, ARUSDT, SFPUSDT, SNXUSDT, 1INCHUSDT, SANDUSDT, IMXUSDT, EGLDUSDT, BATUSDT, DYDXUSDT, ZENUSDT, RSRUSDT, GALAUSDT, QTUMUSDT, DGBUSDT, YFIUSDT

Phase 2 cells (inactive until their own Coen-gated commit): timeframes 1h, 4h, 12h on the same assets

Phase 3 cells (inactive until their own Coen-gated commit): timeframes 15m, 30m on the same assets

The assets are listed in manifest order, and the same 76 are used in every phase. Phase 1 is active from the registry entry of this note. Phase 2 and phase 3 are not active at this entry: each is activated only by its own commit, which Coen decides. The grid is 76 assets by 6 timeframes, 456 cells in all, and 76 of them are active now. A phase 2 or phase 3 cell whose own first bar falls after 2022-12-31 is excluded when its phase is activated and is named in that phase's note; an exclusion never adds a cell.

THE EXCLUDED ASSETS. Each is the ticker followed by USDT. The first bar is the date of its first daily bar, first_1d_utc in data/crypto_universe_manifest.json. Ten have a first bar in 2024 and fourteen have one between 2023-03-17 and 2023-12-15. All 24 fall after 2022-12-31.

Excluded assets (24, not swept): ENA first bar 2024-04-02, ETHFI first bar 2024-03-18, JUP first bar 2024-01-31, PYTH first bar 2024-02-02, RENDER first bar 2024-07-26, STRK first bar 2024-02-20, TAO first bar 2024-04-11, WIF first bar 2024-03-05, ZK first bar 2024-06-17, ZRO first bar 2024-06-20, GAS first bar 2023-03-17, GLM first bar 2023-03-17, PROM first bar 2023-03-17, ARB first bar 2023-03-23, SUI first bar 2023-05-03, FLOKI first bar 2023-05-05, PEPE first bar 2023-05-05, PENDLE first bar 2023-07-03, WLD first bar 2023-07-24, SEI first bar 2023-08-15, TIA first bar 2023-10-31, ORDI first bar 2023-11-07, JTO first bar 2023-12-07, BONK first bar 2023-12-15

WHAT IS FIXED AND WHAT IS OPEN. The set of cells is fixed by this note. Only the timing of phases 2 and 3 is open. Nothing outside this grid can be added: not an asset, not a timeframe, not one of the 24 excluded assets, and not a cell of an asset that listed later. A pair that is delisted or halted is RETIRED by a new note that names it. A retirement never adds a cell. Every strategy registered on the retired pair stays on the chain.

THE POOLED PATH IS RETIRED. From this entry on no new pooled BTCUSD+ETHUSD spec is proposed. Every pooled strategy registered before this entry stays on the chain and re-simulates. Nothing about them is re-judged.

WHAT COUNTS. Each cell is its own counted trial. Activating a phase adds its cells to what is searched. More registrations at a fixed bar is arithmetic about the denominator, never evidence of edge.

payload.claim: MYR Group (MYRG), despite strong revenue growth, a 6.8% EBITDA margin, and net cash, was predicted to be vulnerable to downside because it traded at an elevated valuation of 23.4x EV/EBITDA and 29.1x forward P/E, with risk amplified if project timing slipped or the Valley acquisition took longer to integrate than expected.
payload.quote: I rated MYR Group a Sell because I thought the stock was already pricing in a lot of good news: strong revenue growth, a 6.8% EBITDA margin, and net cash, but also a valuation of 23.4x EV/EBITDA and 29.1x forward P/E. My view was that the downside case was easier to trigger than the upside case, especially if project timing slipped or the Valley acquisition took longer to integrate than expected.

source.title: The Scorecard: 3 Month Update: MYRG Sell — Correct so far

testability.notes: Qualitative execution-risk factors (project timing, acquisition integration) are harder to quantify with standard market data than the valuation multiples.

payload.claim: Shorting MYRG from its entry price of $391.51 on 2026-07-17 to $280.16 on 2026-10-16 would have returned 28.4%, consistent with the original Sell thesis based on valuation concerns.
payload.quote: Over this tracking window, following the Sell would have earned 28.4%, which means the short case has worked. MYRG has fallen from 391.51 to 280.16, so the market has not rewarded the valuation multiple I was worried about.

source.title: The Scorecard: 3 Month Update: MYRG Sell — Correct so far

data_required: MYRG daily closing price history from 2026-07-17 to 2026-10-16

payload.claim: SDGR was overvalued relative to its cash generation profile, as evidenced by a 56.9% gross margin combined with operating cash flow of -$126.9M TTM, an EV/Revenue multiple of 3.9x, and a P/S multiple of 5.1x, which was the basis for a Sell rating.
payload.quote: I argued that SDGR was still priced for growth that its cash generation had not earned, even though the platform itself looked solid. My sell case leaned on the gap between a healthy 56.9% gross margin and the much weaker cash profile, especially operating cash flow of -$126.9M TTM and a valuation of 3.9x EV/Revenue and 5.1x P/S.

source.title: The Scorecard: 2 Month Update: SDGR Sell — Incorrect so far

data_required: SDGR EV/Revenue and P/S historical multiples
testability.notes: Single-name case study; generalizable version would require screening a broader universe for similar margin/cash-flow/valuation profiles.

payload.claim: The sell thesis on SDGR would be invalidated (warranting a more constructive view) if SDGR's free cash flow turned positive and its revenue growth rate re-accelerated.
payload.quote: I also said I would only get more constructive if free cash flow turned positive and revenue growth re-accelerated.

source.title: The Scorecard: 2 Month Update: SDGR Sell — Incorrect so far

data_required: SDGR free cash flow by quarter
SDGR revenue growth rate by quarter
SDGR stock price around FCF/growth inflection points

payload.quote: If SDGR keeps advancing while peers remain mixed, that would further weaken my view that the valuation was detached from fundamentals.

source.locator: What Could Still Prove Me Wrong section
source.title: The Scorecard: 2 Month Update: SDGR Sell — Incorrect so far

payload.claim: US term spread measures (10yr-3mo, 10yr-2yr) indicated a high likelihood of recession in 2023-24 due to the large and persistent yield curve inversion observed in 2022.
payload.quote: Focusing on the United States, it’s clear that most term spread measures (10yr-3mo, 10yr-2yr, etc.) indicated a high likelihood of recession in 2023-24, given the large and persistent inversion in 2022.

source.title: The Term Spread and the Case of the Missing 2024 Recession

data_required: US Treasury yield curve data (10yr, 3mo, 2yr rates)

payload.claim: Prior to the 2020 recession, the yield curve was an accurate predictor of recessions in the US, Canada, and Germany, but became less accurate in predicting recessions thereafter.
payload.quote: We confirm that prior to the 2020 recession, the yield curve was an accurate predictor of recessions in the US, Canada, and Germany, but proved less accurate thereafter.

source.title: The Term Spread and the Case of the Missing 2024 Recession

data_required: US, Canada, Germany yield curve data

payload.claim: For the US, adding a term premium variable to term spread recession prediction models does not appreciably improve prediction, while adding expectations of future unemployment does improve prediction.
payload.quote: For the US, accounting for term premia does not improve prediction appreciably, while taking into account expectations of future unemployment does.

source.title: The Term Spread and the Case of the Missing 2024 Recession

payload.claim: Including the debt service ratio in a recession prediction model alongside the term spread reconciles the absence of a recession in 2024 despite the strong yield curve inversion at the end of 2022, for both the US and Germany.
payload.quote: More definitively, in line with Borio, et al. (2020), we find inclusion of the debt service ratio reconciles the failure of a recession to appear in 2024 after the strong yield curve inversion observed at the end of 2022, for both the US and Germany.

source.title: The Term Spread and the Case of the Missing 2024 Recession

data_required: US and Germany term spread data

payload.claim: In a term-spread-based recession prediction regression, the pseudo R-squared is 0.33 for the pre-2020 sample versus 0.26 for the full sample, adding the ACM term premium estimate does not appreciably change the full-sample pseudo R-squared, and adding the expected change in unemployment rate yields a marginally significant coefficient without materially changing the pseudo R-squared.
payload.quote:
Note that the proportion of variance explained using the term spread is higher in the pre-2020 sample, and lower in the full (0.33 vs. 0.26). Adding in a separate estimated term
premium
(the ACM estimate from the NY Fed) does not appreciably change the full sample result. However, adding in the expected change in unemployment rate (because the Taylor rule implies the Fed funds expected in the future will be lower if markets anticipate a slowdown/recession) does result in a marginally significant coefficient for this variable (although the pseudo R
2
 is essentially unchanged).

source.title: The Term Spread and the Case of the Missing 2024 Recession

payload.claim: Including the debt service ratio (DSR) as a proxy for the financial cycle in the full-sample recession prediction regression raises the pseudo R-squared appreciably to 0.57 and produces the best fit among specifications tested, correctly predicting the 1990-91 and 2008-09 recessions with no false positives.
payload.quote: Only inclusion of a proxy for the financial cycle — the debt service ratio (DSR) — raises the proportion of variance explained appreciably, to 0.57. It also turns out that the best “fit” — in the sense of no false positives, while catching the recessions of 1990-91, 2008-09, is the equation incorporating the DSR (teal line in figure below, marked &DSR).

source.title: The Term Spread and the Case of the Missing 2024 Recession

payload.claim: When the DSR-augmented recession prediction model is estimated only on pre-2020 data, it correctly predicts the 1990-91, 2001, and 2008-09 recessions but does not predict the 2020 pandemic recession or a recession in 2024.
payload.quote: The finding that the DSR’s inclusion helps in accurately predicting recessions holds true even if one restricts the estimation period to pre-2020. Then the 1990-91, 2001, and 2008-09 recessions are predicted, but not the 2020 pandemic one (nor a 2024 recession).

source.title: The Term Spread and the Case of the Missing 2024 Recession

payload.claim: A recession prediction model that includes the expected change in the unemployment rate and uses the Fed funds rate instead of the 3-month rate reduces the estimated probability of a 2024 recession below a 40% threshold while still correctly predicting previous recessions except for 2008-09.

payload.claim: Following Ben Bernanke's May 2013 tapering announcement, emerging market countries with stronger macro fundamentals (current accounts, reserves, external debt) experienced larger currency depreciation, larger stock market drops, and sharper increases in spreads than fragile emerging countries.
payload.quote: Aizenman, Binici and Hutchinson (2014) showed that, in opposition to what could be expected, the effects were larger on emerging countries with stronger macro fundamentals (current accounts, reserves, external debt) than on fragile countries. Indeed they observe larger depreciation, larger drops in the stock market and a sharp increase in spreads.

payload.claim: A systematic strategy whose regime-conditional Sharpe ratios, computed by segmenting backtest returns via an HMM or rolling volatility filter, diverge by more than 0.8-1.0 Sharpe units across regimes should be classified as regime-dependent and managed accordingly in live trading.
payload.quote: Segment your historical backtest returns by detected regime state. Use a simple HMM or rolling volatility filter to assign regime labels, then compute Sharpe, maximum drawdown, and win rate within each regime. If your strategy performance diverges dramatically by regime (a spread of more than 0.8–1.0 Sharpe units), you have a regime-dependent strategy and need to account for this in live trading.

payload.claim: For characteristic-managed portfolios traded by machine-learning methods and for individual stocks with persistently differing factor loadings, a conditional asset pricing model with only a few factors produces an unconditional return covariance matrix with infinitely many diverging eigenvalues rather than the standard eigenvalue cliff (few large eigenvalues followed by a bounded bulk).
payload.quote: We show that, generically, this view removes the cliff: a conditional model with a few factors is, unconditionally, an infinite-factor model in which infinitely many eigenvalues diverge. This holds for the characteristic-managed portfolios that machine-learning methods trade, and for individual stocks whose loadings differ persistently across firms.

source.title: Infinite Factor Structure in Conditional Asset Pricing -- by Mikhail Chernov, Bryan T. Kelly, Semyon Malamud, Johannes Schwab

data_required: estimated unconditional return covariance matrix and its eigenvalue spectrum
testability.notes: This is a theoretical/structural claim about covariance matrix spectra; testing requires constructing large covariance matrices from stock or ML-characteristic portfolio returns and examining eigenvalue decay.

payload.claim: Even when the unconditional return covariance matrix exhibits infinitely many diverging eigenvalues, the maximal attainable Sharpe ratio remains finite provided conditional expected returns satisfy a no-asymptotic-arbitrage condition.
payload.quote: Yet as long as conditional expected returns admit no asymptotic arbitrage, the maximal Sharpe ratio stays finite.

payload.claim: For generic expected returns, infinitely many principal components of the return covariance matrix carry priced risk, so restricting asset pricing or portfolio construction to a finite number of principal components omits priced risk that a few-factor/PCA approach would miss.
payload.quote: For generic expected returns, infinitely many components are priced, so no finite set of principal components spans expected returns. Reducing returns to a few principal components therefore discards priced risk.

payload.claim: Daily returns of the German DAX index and daily returns of its implied volatility index VDAX had a correlation of -0.72 over the period from November 16, 2005 to April 17, 2014.
payload.quote:
German DAX returns (y-axis) vs. its implied volatility index returns VDAX return (x-axis) from Nov. 16th 2005 until Apr. 17th 2014 (Data available at www.quandl.com/DAROU/12N-Dax-and-VDax )
This scatter plot shows a “x” for all trading days in the past 8 years with VDAX return as x-postion and DAX return as y-postion. This plot shows that there is a close relationship between these two. In fact, a little computation shows that they have correlation of -0.72 which is very high.

source.locator: section: 'German DAX and VDAX are highly correlated'
source.title: VDAX revisited – Implied volatility return vs. Index Return

testability.notes: Correlation computed on daily returns per the scatter plot description; exact return definition (log vs simple) not specified.

payload.claim: Large spikes in the DAX index are accompanied by opposite-direction spikes in the VDAX implied volatility index rather than same-direction spikes.
payload.quote: We can see that for each spike in the red curve of DAX, there is an opposite spike in VDAX. This is surprising since we would expect that a large rise in DAX would also cause a large rise in implied volatility, namely VDAX. But, this is not the case.

source.locator: section: 'German DAX and VDAX are highly correlated'
source.title: VDAX revisited – Implied volatility return vs. Index Return

testability.notes: Qualitative observation from a time series chart; 'spike' is not precisely defined.

payload.claim: For traded DAX options, put options further in-the-money trade at a higher implied volatility than the at-the-money implied volatility represented by VDAX.
payload.quote: By the way, this is a well-known effect: The implied volatility skew. Looking at the traded options, the put options further in-the-money already trade at a higher implied volatility – VDAX represents at-the-money options only.

source.locator: final section, after scatter plot discussion
source.title: VDAX revisited – Implied volatility return vs. Index Return

data_required: DAX option implied volatility surface by moneyness
testability.notes: Stated as a general well-known effect rather than a new empirical finding specific to this document's data.

payload.claim: Because DAX returns and VDAX returns are negatively correlated, call option buyers on the DAX experience offsetting time-value decay from falling implied volatility when the index rises, while put option buyers benefit from rising implied volatility when the index falls.
payload.quote: Consider buying a call option: Now, the stock price rises. And the call option price rises because your option is deeper in-the-money: Its asset price minus strike price is higher. But, at the same time, the time value decays because the implied volatility goes down. So, for call option buyers this might be an issue. For Put option buyers, this effect works in their favour. The implied volatility rises when the asset price drops.

source.title: VDAX revisited – Implied volatility return vs. Index Return

data_required: DAX call and put option prices/implied volatilities
testability.notes: Theoretical reasoning derived from the negative DAX-VDAX correlation rather than a directly backtested rule.

payload.claim: A stock showing improving revenue (e.g. PENN's Q2 2026 revenue of $1.9B) but still carrying heavy leverage (net debt/EBITDA of 11.7x) and negative levered free cash flow is a Sell candidate, and the bearish view should only be revised toward Hold once levered free cash flow turns positive for two consecutive quarters.
payload.quote: I rated PENN a Sell because I thought the revenue recovery was real but not enough to offset the balance-sheet strain and weak cash conversion. My original call leaned on the fact that Q2 2026 revenue had improved to $1.9B, yet debt was still $11.1B, net debt sat at 11.7x EBITDA, and levered free cash flow was still negative. I also said I would only get more constructive if levered free cash flow turned positive for two straight quarters.

source.title: The Scorecard: 2 Month Update: PENN Sell — Correct so far

data_required: PENN quarterly levered free cash flow

payload.claim: A bearish thesis on PENN driven by weak cash conversion and leverage would be invalidated if the stock re-rates higher at the same time that levered free cash flow and debt metrics (net debt/EBITDA) improve together.
payload.quote: I would be wrong if PENN starts producing positive levered free cash flow for two consecutive quarters, because that would directly validate the condition I set for moving toward a Hold. I would also reassess if the company shows that the current revenue base can support materially better cash conversion without relying on additional leverage. If the stock were to re-rate higher while those cash-flow and debt metrics improve together, my original bearish case would no longer be intact.

payload.quote: To test this, I compare 12 trend indicators within the same systematic sector rotation framework, using daily US sector ETF data from June 2009 through October 2026.

payload.quote: The investment universe consists of the 11 Select Sector SPDR ETFs, including technology (XLK), financials (XLF), energy (XLE), healthcare (XLV), and the other major S&P 500 sectors.

source.title: Which Trend Indicator Works Best for Sector Rotation?

payload.claim: A sector rotation strategy that each month-end ranks eligible Select Sector SPDR ETFs by a trend score, equally invests in the three highest-ranked sectors, rebalances at the next month's first-trading-day opening price, and deducts a 5 basis point one-way transaction cost can be backtested and compared across different trend indicators.
payload.quote:
At each month-end, calculate a trend score for every eligible sector ETF.
Rank the sectors from strongest to weakest according to the selected indicator.
Invest equally in the three highest-ranked sectors.
Rebalance at the opening price on the first trading day of the following month.
Deduct a one-way transaction cost of 5 basis points.

payload.claim: In the original April 2025 OFR analysis using a 2022 three-day pilot collection of non-centrally cleared bilateral repo (NCCBR) data, newly cleared repos subject to the SEC central clearing rule would not have changed the level of SOFR but could widen the tails of its rate distribution.
payload.quote: It found that newly cleared repos would not have changed SOFR but could widen the tails of its rate distribution.

source.title: An Update on How the Treasury Clearing Rule for Repo Might Affect SOFR

testability.notes: References prior analysis's finding, endorsed/updated by this document.

payload.claim: Applying the SEC Treasury repo clearing rule and FRBNY SOFR eligibility criteria to OFR's NCCBR collection over the last year, the clearing mandate could add slightly more than $500 billion in daily transaction volume to SOFR, compared to the pilot-based estimate of about $85 billion.
payload.quote: Under these assumptions, the clearing mandate could add slightly more than $500 billion in daily transaction volume to SOFR. The pilot-based estimate was about $85 billion.

source.title: An Update on How the Treasury Clearing Rule for Repo Might Affect SOFR

payload.claim: Under the assumption that all repo volume subject to the SEC clearing requirement is centrally cleared through FICC's DVP service and SOFR calculation details are unchanged, the hypothetical SOFR could be 1 basis point higher than the published SOFR rate while its volatility remains roughly unchanged.
payload.quote: The hypothetical SOFR could increase by 1 basis point higher than the published rate, and its volatility is roughly unchanged, assuming details of the SOFR calculation is left unchanged.

source.title: An Update on How the Treasury Clearing Rule for Repo Might Affect SOFR

payload.claim: In an extreme scenario where all money market fund repo volume shifts from clearing through Sponsored DVP to Sponsored General Collateral (GC), SOFR could see a relative shift of up to 2 basis points above historical levels.
payload.quote: Under an extreme scenario in which all these funds’ volume shifted from Sponsored DVP moves to Sponsored GC, SOFR could see a relative shift of up to 2 basis points above historical levels.

source.title: An Update on How the Treasury Clearing Rule for Repo Might Affect SOFR

data_required: money market fund repo clearing volume by segment (Sponsored DVP vs Sponsored GC)

payload.claim: The SOFR calculation methodology's specials trim, which excludes a percentage of the lowest volume-weighted DVP repo rates, changed from a 25% threshold in the original analysis to a 20% threshold in this update.
payload.quote: Unlike the original, this update uses the current specials trim, which excludes the bottom 20% of volume-weighted DVP repo rates. The original analysis used the 25% “specials” threshold procedure.

source.title: An Update on How the Treasury Clearing Rule for Repo Might Affect SOFR

testability.notes: Methodological detail that affects how SOFR estimates are constructed, testable against published SOFR construction rules.
